how-often-to-recheck-vendor-pages.html.text:
← Vendor Change Watch

How often should you re-check a vendor's terms and privacy pages?

A “last updated” date tells you a page changed at some point — not what changed, not whether it matters, and not whether it happened before or after you last actually read it. Below is a practical cadence by vendor risk, and the events worth checking on regardless of schedule.

A cadence by risk, not one calendar for every vendor

Checking every vendor on the same schedule either wastes review time on low-risk tools or lets a high-risk one go unwatched for as long as the slowest tier allows. A vendor that stores regulated data, acts as a subprocessor to your own product, or sits deep in a supply chain carries more exposure from a quiet change than a marketing tool with no access to your data at all.

Vendor risk tierExampleSuggested cadence
High — processes regulated data, or is itself a subprocessor in your data pathPayment processor, a data processor named in your own DPA, an infrastructure hostMonthly
Medium — core SaaS vendor with broad account or data access, not itself regulatedCRM, support desk, analytics platform your team logs into dailyQuarterly
Low — limited or no access to your dataA marketing site tool, an internal wiki with no customer dataTwice a year, or after a triggering event below

These are starting points, not a compliance requirement — your own contract, regulator, or internal policy may set a stricter cadence for a given vendor. Tighten the tier rather than loosen it if the two disagree.

Four events worth an off-schedule check

A fixed cadence misses changes that cluster around specific events. Check outside the normal schedule when:

  • A security incident or breach is disclosed involving the vendor or one of its own subprocessors — terms and subprocessor lists are often revised in the same news cycle.
  • The vendor is acquired or merges — ownership changes frequently bring rewritten data-handling, retention, or subprocessor terms within weeks.
  • A pricing or plan change ships — terms edits sometimes land in the same release as a pricing announcement, and get less scrutiny riding alongside it.
  • A contract renews, or a procurement review starts — capture the current text on record regardless of when it last changed, so the review has a dated snapshot rather than a memory of what the terms used to say.

Why the date on the page is not the signal

A “last updated” date is the vendor's own claim about when the page changed, worded however they choose to word it, and it is common for the same date to cover a formatting fix and a substantive clause rewrite alike. It also says nothing about when you last read the page, so a date from six months ago could sit in front of a change you have already seen, or behind one you have not. What actually answers the question is a diff against your own last capture: the section that changed, the words that moved, and the two timestamps of when each capture happened.

A first capture of a page is reported as captured, never as “unchanged” — there is nothing yet to compare it against, and a check with no basis for comparison must never read as stability. See Vendor Change Watch to capture a page and get that diff on your own schedule, in the browser or from the command line.

Common questions

How often should I re-check a vendor's terms of service?

There is no single right answer, but a practical default is to match the check to risk: vendors that touch regulated data, hold a subprocessor role, or sit deep in your supply chain get checked monthly; core SaaS vendors with broad access to your data get checked quarterly; low-risk tools with no data access get checked twice a year or simply after a news event names them. A calendar reminder is enough to trigger the check — it is the fetch and the comparison that are worth automating, not the schedule itself.

Does a vendor's own 'last updated' date tell me anything?

It tells you the page changed at some point, not what changed, not whether the change affects you, and not whether it happened before or after you last actually read the page. Many vendors also bump that date on formatting-only edits, so treating it as a signal either over-alerts on cosmetic changes or, worse, trains a reviewer to stop trusting the date at all. A source-linked diff against your own last capture answers the question the date cannot: what changed since I looked.

What should trigger an immediate re-check outside the normal schedule?

Four events are worth an off-cycle check regardless of a vendor's normal cadence: a public security incident or breach disclosure involving the vendor or one of its own subprocessors; an acquisition or merger, which frequently rewrites data-handling and subprocessor terms; a pricing or plan change announcement, which sometimes ships alongside quiet terms edits in the same release; and a contract renewal or procurement review, where you want the current text on record regardless of when it last changed.

Should every vendor get the same re-check cadence?

No. A vendor with no access to your data and no subprocessor role carries a different risk than one that stores regulated records or sits in your product's own data path. Checking both on the same calendar either wastes review time on the low-risk vendor or, more commonly, lets the high-risk one go unchecked for as long as the slowest tier in a flat schedule.

Want the mechanics of the diff itself, not the cadence? See the tool's own FAQ, or how this compares to a general-purpose watcher on this tool vs. changedetection.io.

No warranty. This free tool and this page are provided as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, procurement, or security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a real contract review. The cadence above is a starting point, not a guarantee that following it would have caught any specific change. You are responsible for setting a review schedule appropriate to your own vendors and obligations.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, export your reports and run the CLI yourself.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — optional support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

index.html.text:
VENDOR CHANGE WATCH · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

See exactly what changed in a vendor's terms.

A vendor edits its subprocessor list, stretches a retention window, or shortens the notice period it owes you — and the only signal is a “last updated” date. Paste the page here to capture it. Paste it again next month and this page shows you the clause that moved, word by word, with the source URL and both timestamps on the report.

Nothing is uploaded and there is no account. Captures stay in this browser, on this device.

Capture a page

Fill in the vendor, page type and source URL, paste the page, and capture. Your first capture of a page is stored, not diffed — there is nothing to compare it to yet.

Report

Watchlist

Pages you have captured in this browser. Two captures are kept per page — the pair a diff needs. Re-capture a page to compare it against the one before.

Watch them automatically instead

This page needs you to remember to come back. The command-line version of the same tool does not: it fetches the pages you configure on your machine, on whatever schedule you already run — cron, launchd, a CI job — and prints the same report. Same diff logic, same three statuses.

pip install -e ventures/vendor-change-watch

vendor-watch add --vendor "Acme SaaS" \
  --url https://acme.example/legal/subprocessors --type subprocessors
vendor-watch check

A failed or blocked fetch is reported as inconclusive, never as “no change”. Everything lives under ~/.vendor-watch — delete the directory to delete all of it — and VENDOR_WATCH_NO_TELEMETRY=1 turns off even the local counters. Run vendor-watch --help for the full command set.

What this answers

  • Which clause actually moved? Changes are grouped under the heading they happened in, and shown word by word rather than as two walls of prose.
  • Did they add a subprocessor? A heading that appears in the newer capture and not the older one is reported as added, with its text.
  • Can I put this in a ticket? The Markdown report carries the vendor, the page type, the source URL and both capture timestamps, so the evidence travels with the finding.
  • What it does not answer: whether a change matters, whether it breaches your contract, or whether the vendor is compliant with anything. It reports text, and you decide.

Common questions

Why can't this fetch the vendor's page for me?

Browsers refuse cross-origin reads of another site's pages, so nothing served from here can fetch acme.example's terms on your behalf without a server in the middle — and that server would see every URL you watch. Rather than run it, this page asks you to paste. The CLI above does fetch, on your own machine, where no third party is involved.

Does the text I paste leave my browser?

No. Parsing, storage and diffing all happen in this page. Captures are kept in this browser's local storage on your own device and are never uploaded; “Delete all captures” removes them.

Does a detected change mean the vendor broke a commitment?

No. This reports what changed in the text you captured, with the source URL and both timestamps. It is not legal advice, does not review contracts, and does not assert that a vendor is or is not compliant with anything. You decide what a change means.

Why does the first capture not show a diff?

There is nothing to compare it against. A first capture is reported as captured, never as “unchanged” — a check with no basis for comparison must not look like stability. Paste the page again later and the second capture produces the report.

What counts as a section?

Text is grouped under the nearest preceding heading. Pasted HTML uses its real h1–h6 headings; pasted plain text treats a short standalone line above a paragraph as a heading. Anything before the first heading is grouped under (page).

Is this the same as the command-line tool?

It shares the diff logic and the exact status vocabulary — observed, inconclusive and unknown mean the same thing in both. The CLI adds the part a browser cannot do: it fetches the pages you configure on a schedule from your own machine, so you are not the one remembering to check.

Not sure how often to check a given vendor? See how often should you re-check a vendor's terms and privacy pages.

Already using a general-purpose page watcher? See this tool vs. changedetection.io. Still checking vendor pages by memory? See this tool vs. checking vendor pages by hand.

Already holding two dated JSON snapshots of the same vendor page? The vendor change evidence tool compares a before and after snapshot into a portable review record — nothing uploaded.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, procurement, or security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a real contract review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use, including reliance on a report that showed no change or on a change it did not detect.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, export your reports and run the CLI yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. Your data is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (page_captured, report_built, example_loaded, report_copied, report_downloaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button above. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Free and open source. If it caught a vendor change before it mattered, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Want a command-line diff you can run from cron? See Vendor Watch.

vs-changedetection-io.html.text:
← Vendor Change Watch

This tool vs. changedetection.io

Two different shapes: changedetection.io is a general-purpose, open-source webpage change monitor you point at any URL. This tool watches only the vendor legal and security pages a practitioner already tracks by hand, and its status vocabulary — observed, inconclusive, unknown — is built so a failed or blocked check can never quietly read as “nothing changed.”

What each tool is for

changedetection.io is a well-known open-source webpage change-detection tool. You give it any URL — a product page, a price listing, a news page, a vendor's terms, anything — and it watches for changes, with a browser extension for picking exactly the element on the page to watch, visual/screenshot diffing, and a wide range of notification integrations (email, Slack, Discord, webhooks, and more). It is self-hosted, or available as a paid hosted service for people who do not want to run their own instance. It is built to be one tool that watches many kinds of pages for many kinds of reasons.

This tool does one job on purpose: it watches the vendor pages a security, procurement, or privacy practitioner already cares about — terms of service, privacy policy, subprocessor list, security page — and reports a source-linked, section-by-section, word-level diff when the text changes. It shares its diff logic and its exact status vocabulary between the free CLI and a try-it-now browser page: a snapshot that did not capture cleanly is inconclusive, a pair that looks like it describes different pages is unknown, and neither may ever collapse to “no change” — a failed check that looks like stability is the one defect this venture exists to avoid. It makes no claim to interpret what a change means; every report carries the source URL and both capture timestamps and leaves the judgment to the practitioner.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to watch many different kinds of pages (pricing, stock, news, vendor pages) in one tool with rich notification routing.changedetection.io — built as a general-purpose watcher across arbitrary pages.
I want a purpose-built watcher for vendor terms, privacy, subprocessor, and security pages with a status that never hides a failed check as “unchanged.”This tool — free, source-linked, and built specifically for that failure mode.
I want to try a diff instantly, without installing or hosting anything, by pasting a page I already have open.This tool's browser page — paste, come back later, paste again.
I want a browser extension to visually pick the exact element on a page to watch.changedetection.io — built for that workflow across arbitrary pages.
I want automated notifications routed to Slack, Discord, email, or a webhook when any watched page changes.changedetection.io — that integration breadth is not this tool's job.
I want to run scheduled checks on my own machine with no server, no account, and a CLI built around the same diff logic as the browser page.This tool's CLI (vendor-watch check) — local storage under ~/.vendor-watch, nothing uploaded.

Most practitioners get different value from each: changedetection.io as a broad, general-purpose page monitor with rich alerting when the surface to watch is wide and varied, and a narrow tool like this one when the surface is specifically the vendor legal and security pages a security, procurement, or privacy review already depends on, and a missed or blocked check must never be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nothing here is a claim that changedetection.io lacks reliability or accuracy — it is a claim about which tool is built around which failure mode.

This tool needs no account, no hosting, and no server to try: the comparison page runs entirely in your browser, and the CLI's stored data never leaves your own machine.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or changedetection.io?

They overlap but aim at different jobs. changedetection.io is a general-purpose, open-source webpage change monitor: point it at any URL — a product page, a stock listing, a news page, a vendor's terms — and it watches for changes, with a browser extension, visual element selection, and a wide range of notification integrations (email, Slack, Discord, webhooks, and more). It is self-hosted (or run as a paid hosted service) and built to watch many kinds of pages for many kinds of teams. Vendor Change Watch is narrower on purpose: it watches only the vendor pages a security, procurement, or privacy practitioner already tracks by hand (terms, privacy policy, subprocessor list, security page), reports a source-linked, section-by-section, word-level diff, and uses a status vocabulary — observed, inconclusive, unknown — that a failed or blocked fetch can never collapse into “no change.” If you want one tool to watch many kinds of pages with rich notification routing, changedetection.io is the better fit. If you want a free, purpose-built watcher for vendor legal and security pages that a practitioner can also try instantly in the browser with a pasted page, this tool is the narrower, simpler fit.

Is this page affiliated with changedetection.io?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by changedetection.io or its maintainers. changedetection.io is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.

Does changedetection.io have the inconclusive/unknown distinction this tool has?

Not as a first-class concept in its reporting the way this tool does. changedetection.io is built to alert on detected change across arbitrary pages; this tool's specific design constraint is that a failed, blocked, or mismatched capture must never look like “nothing changed” to a practitioner relying on it for a vendor's legal or security commitments, so it reports inconclusive or unknown separately from a real observed diff. That is a narrower, domain-specific guarantee, not a claim that changedetection.io lacks reliability features generally.

Open Vendor Change Watch to try your own vendor page.

No warranty. This free tool is provided as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, procurement, or security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It reports what changed in the text of pages you configured; it does not assert that a vendor is or is not compliant with anything. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it.

Nothing leaves your browser. This page makes no live connection to changedetection.io and no live comparison against it — it is a static page describing publicly documented facts about changedetection.io's product category.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — optional GitHub Sponsors support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-vendor-pages-by-hand.html.text:
← Vendor Change Watch

This tool vs. checking vendor pages by hand

Names no specific company or product — this compares against the manual habit nearly every practitioner already has: opening a vendor's terms, privacy, or subprocessor page from time to time and eyeballing whether it looks different from what you remember.

What checking by hand actually does

Revisiting a vendor page by hand is free and needs no tool, which is exactly why it is the default. You open the page, skim it, and compare it against your memory of the last time you read it. If nothing jumps out, you move on assuming nothing changed.

That method has three failure modes this tool exists to close. First, memory is not a diff: a single clause rewritten in place — a retention window stretched, a notice period shortened, a subprocessor swapped for another with the same category label — reads the same at a glance as the version you remember, because nothing preserved the exact wording to compare against. Second, a failed check looks identical to a clean one: a page that timed out, redirected, or was blocked by the vendor's own bot protection shows you nothing, and "I saw nothing wrong" and "I saw nothing at all" produce the same blank result in your head. Third, there is no record afterward — no source URL, no timestamp, no before-and-after text — so six months later neither you nor a reviewer can reconstruct what the page said the last time anyone actually looked.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to know if a vendor's page has changed at all, and I am willing to re-read the whole thing from memory.Checking by hand — free, and works if the change is large enough to notice.
I want to know exactly which clause changed, word for word, without relying on memory.This tool — a section-by-section, word-level diff between two captures.
I want to tell a genuinely unchanged page apart from a check that silently failed.This tool — a failed or blocked capture is reported as inconclusive, never as "no change."
I want evidence I can put in a ticket: a source URL, both timestamps, and the exact before/after text.This tool — the report is built from what was actually captured, not from what someone recalls.
I want to run scheduled checks without remembering to revisit the page myself.This tool's CLI — fetches on your own machine, on whatever schedule you already run.

Checking by hand is not wrong so much as unverifiable: a practitioner doing it carefully, every single time, would eventually catch most large changes. What it structurally cannot do is prove a check happened, prove what it found, or catch a change smaller than what memory retains — and this tool's whole design, on both the browser page and the CLI, is built around closing exactly those three gaps for free.

This tool needs no account, no hosting, and no server to try: the comparison page runs entirely in your browser, and the CLI's stored data never leaves your own machine.

Common questions

What does checking a vendor's page by hand actually catch?

It catches a change large enough to jump out against your memory of the page — a rewritten heading, a new paragraph, a page that looks obviously different in layout or length. It does not catch a single clause edited in place inside a page that otherwise reads the same, because nothing about a by-hand look preserves what the page actually said last time you read it.

Why is “I checked and it looked the same” not proof of anything?

Because a page that failed to load, redirected somewhere else, or was blocked by the vendor's own bot protection can look exactly like a page that never changed — you scroll, you do not see the change you were looking for, and you move on having actually looked at nothing. A by-hand check has no way to distinguish those two outcomes from each other, and no record afterward of which one happened.

Can I put a by-hand check in a ticket as evidence?

Only as a note that you looked, on a given date, and did not personally notice anything. That is weaker evidence than a reviewer, an auditor, or your own future self usually needs — it carries no source URL, no before/after text, and no independent way to confirm which version of the page you were actually looking at.

Open Vendor Change Watch to try your own vendor page.

No warranty. This free tool is provided as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, procurement, or security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It reports what changed in the text of pages you configured; it does not assert that a vendor is or is not compliant with anything. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice.
